title: The temple, explained

segments.voice: Yesterday, rest: A, U, M, and the quiet after. Your line was put it down. What was the last thing in your mind before you slept? Day one hundred and thirty-two.

You're standing outside a Hindu temple for the first time. Maybe it's a grand carved one, maybe a converted warehouse off the highway with a painted sign. People are going in and out, easy and relaxed. And you're frozen at the steps, full of questions. Do I need to be Hindu? What do I wear? Where do I go first? What if I do something wrong in front of everyone? For three weeks you've practiced at home: the shrine, the flame, the food. This week you step out of the house and into the big one. Today: the temple, explained.
screen: `FROZEN AT THE STEPS.` → `WHERE DO I GO FIRST?` → `A NEW WEEK: TEMPLE AND COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: The Hindi word is mandir, from the Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house. That's the key. A temple is understood as a home where the divine lives, in the form of the murti, the sacred image, which has been ritually installed and is cared for every day: woken, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night. So you're not walking into an auditorium. You're visiting someone's house. That's why the first thing everybody does is take off their shoes. There's usually a rack by the door. Many people wash their hands, sometimes their feet. Then, often, they ring the bell hanging at the entrance: your ghanta, announcing that you've arrived. At the heart of the temple is the innermost shrine, called the garbhagriha, the womb-house: small, often dark, lit by lamps, with the main image inside. In many temples, only priests go in. Everyone else stands at the threshold, looks, and bows. Above it rises the tower, which you can often see from the street. Many temples have smaller shrines too, for other forms of the divine, and people visit them in turn. There's often no single service everyone arrives for: most people come and go when they like, though arti times draw a crowd. A few quiet customs: dress modestly, don't point your feet at the shrine when you sit, and ask before taking photos. Most temples welcome visitors of any background; a few famous ones admit only Hindus. And if you're unsure, do what a guest does anywhere. Shoes off, watch, and follow.
screen: `MANDIR — A DWELLING, A HOUSE.` · `THE MURTI, CARED FOR DAILY.` · `SHOES OFF, BELL, THRESHOLD.` · `THE GARBHAGRIHA: THE WOMB-HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and walk in, slowly, in your mind. You reach the steps. You bend down and take off your shoes, and feel the cool floor under your feet. Maybe you rinse your hands. You reach up and ring the bell, and listen to it fade. Now you walk forward, toward the lamplight. Ahead is a small, dim doorway, and inside it, the image, lit by flames. You stop at the threshold. If you'd like, you put your hands together. And you just stand there, a guest in the house. The bell holds the time.
Mandir. The Hindu temple: a dwelling, a house where the divine is cared for every day, and where you enter as a guest, shoes off. Today's word.
Your line: shoes off. Today, when you walk into your own home, take a breath at the door as you take your shoes off, and treat it as a place where someone lives. Day one hundred and thirty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Hindu church.
what it means: a house where the divine lives as the murti, cared for every day, entered as a guest, shoes off.

what a scholar hears: the temple is built around the garbhagriha, beneath the tower (shikhara in northern styles, vimana in southern, with gopuram gateways); the murti is ritually installed and served daily through the upacharas.
